author: Wren Aldous & Piotr Sable
blurb: A municipal utility inspector walks up a stairwell to take a reading and finds that the building has opinions about being measured. Forty pages, stapled, printed on whatever the Ironside press had that month. The one everybody has heard of and nobody has actually read, largely because the film came later and was worse.

chapters.text:
A door. Grey, institutional, half a number missing from it, the ghost of the missing digit still legible in cleaner paint. Nothing else. Just the door, held long enough that you are standing in front of it before anybody arrives.

> Tuesday. The building had been quiet for eleven days, which the district office recorded as "no fault reported."

A man from behind. Municipal tabard, reflective strip across the shoulders gone chalky. A clipboard held down at his side the way a man holds a thing he has carried for twenty years. We do not see his face.

METER READER: Utilities.

Same door. Still shut.

METER READER: Utilities. It's the reading.

A hand comes in from off the page and rests flat on the door. Not knocking. Just resting.

> You do not have to let a meter reader in. You have never had to let a meter reader in. There is no law that says so and there never was. What there is instead is a form, and the form has a box on it, and the box says ACCESS REFUSED, and the box has consequences that nobody has ever written down anywhere you could read them.

---

The door is open. We did not see it open.

Inside, a hallway. Wallpaper in a pattern that was chosen by somebody who is dead. A pram folded against the wall. A bicycle with no chain. The kind of hall that is all objects belonging to people who are elsewhere.

A woman in the kitchen doorway, arms folded, drawn heavier than anything else in the room.

WOMAN: You're not the usual one.
METER READER: No.
WOMAN: Where's the usual one.

He looks at the clipboard. He does not look up.

METER READER: I've got the round.

---

The meter face. Six digits on white drums. The last one is caught between numbers, half of a 4 and half of a 5.

His hand with a pencil, writing the figure on the form. The pencil is blunt. There is a groove worn into his finger.

WOMAN: That's not right.

He keeps writing.

METER READER: It's what it says.
WOMAN: Nobody's been using anything. There's nobody here to use anything.

He looks up, and the tilt of the head has changed, and his shoulder has come down about four millimetres, and it reads as a man deciding whether to say the next thing.

METER READER: I know.

---

> The number had gone up every week for eleven weeks, in a flat where the calendar stopped, and it was his job to write it down, and he had written it down, and he had gone home, and he had come back, and it had gone up again.
chapters.title: The Ground Floor

chapters.text:
The stairwell, looking up: eleven flights of switchback rail receding into a skylight that is not there any more, just the frame and the sky. He is a small figure at the bottom.

> Flat 2. Flat 6. Flat 9. Flat 14.

A door. Grey. Half a number.

METER READER: Utilities.

A different door. Also grey. A different missing digit.

METER READER: Utilities.

A third door, and now the walls are gone from around them, and the doors float on white, and it has stopped being a building and become a rhythm.

METER READER: It's the reading.

---

Thirty-one meter faces, laid out together, each one with its own dirt and its own crack and its own painted-over cabinet. Under each, in the same blunt pencil hand, the figure.

The figures go up. They go up in every flat. They go up in the two flats that are boarded from the outside.

> The district office ran a check on the substation and found it sound. The district office ran a check on the trunk main and found it sound. The district office wrote to the building and the letters came back marked NO SUCH RESIDENT, thirty-one times, which the district office recorded as "no fault reported."

---

Night. A kitchen table, and a man sitting at it with the forms spread out and his hands flat on either side of them. The wallpaper is the pattern chosen by somebody who is dead. The pram is against the wall in the hall.

It is three panels before you work out that the flat is his, and then you go back.

One form, close. The pencil figure. Beside it, in ink, in a different hand, in the margin where nobody is supposed to write: a second figure. Larger.

His hands have not moved.

> He had not written that.

---

The meter cabinet in his own kitchen. Painted over four times. A perfect circle wiped clean in the little glass window.

Closer. Closer. The drums. Six digits, the last one caught between numbers.

Closer still, until we are inside the glass and the drums are the whole page and the halftone has gone strange and wet.

Then the number.

It is a very large number. It is set in a typeface that appears nowhere else in the book. It runs to nineteen digits and no unit is given, and whether the missing unit is the joke or the horror is the thing people still argue about in the shop.

---

He is writing it down.

He is still writing it down.

He is still writing it down. The pencil is shorter.

> It is not the reader's job to be alarmed. It is the reader's job to read.

---

The stairwell again. The same rail, the same absent skylight, except that the figure at the bottom is going up now, and each time we come back he is one flight higher and one size smaller, until he is not in it at all.

The number of flights has not changed.
chapters.title: The Rising Figure

chapters.text:
The top landing. A door that is not grey. It is the only warm colour in the book after the first flat, and on the original run the colour sits two millimetres to the left of the door, which every reprint has faithfully reproduced.

There is no number on it and no space where a number was.

METER READER: Utilities.

Nothing.

METER READER: It's the reading.

Nothing.

He puts his hand flat on the door and rests it there.

---

The room beyond has thirty-one meter cabinets on the walls. Every one painted over four times. Every one with a perfect circle wiped clean. Every one running.

In the middle of the room there is a kitchen table with forms spread out on it and a blunt pencil laid across them, squared to the edge.

There is one chair. There is nobody in it.

The open line the whole book has been drawn in gives out here and goes to crosshatch, thousands of strokes, so dense that on the original press it clogged, and the top third of this page in most surviving copies is a solid grey-black smear that the publisher never fixed and the artist never wanted fixed.

---

He sits down.

He picks up the pencil.

He begins to write.

---

Then the forms. Twenty-four pages of them, one flat to a line, thirty-one lines to a page, in blunt pencil, with no panel and no caption and nobody speaking.

The addresses are real Coldwater addresses. The dates run backwards. On the ninth line of the twenty-second page the handwriting changes for one entry and then changes back, and nobody has ever satisfactorily explained what that entry says.

The thickness of it is doing the work. You feel it in your hand whether you read it or not.

---

His face, small, alone in the top corner of an otherwise empty page.

It is an ordinary face. Fifty-something, tired, shaved yesterday. It is not frightened and it is not haunted and there is nothing behind the eyes that shouldn't be. It is the face of a man at work.

> They send someone every week. They have always sent someone every week. Nothing is wrong with the building.

The door. Grey. Half a number missing, the ghost of the missing digit still legible in cleaner paint.

METER READER: Utilities.

---

> On the inside back cover, in every edition: LETTERS. Write to us. We read everything and we answer what we can. We are told the second issue will be along when it is along.

> There was no second issue.
chapters.title: The Face

source: Scanned from the Mint Condition reading copy, Ironside Street, Coldwater. In-universe fiction.
title: The Meter Reader #1: The Reading
